I've drafted notes for verses 1–22. I couldn't find anything for verse 23, and the material for sections 2 and 3 is thin. I ran out of searches before I could read the Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, modern-scholarship or Catholic/Orthodox sites directly, so those gaps are listed at the end.

## Matthew 21:1–22: research notes

**v. 1**
- Bethphage and Bethany lie on the east side of the Mount of Olives. No one knows exactly where Bethphage was; most place it on the southeast slope, about 1.5 miles from Jerusalem. Jesus stayed overnight at Bethany during His final week. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says Jesus knew He would be arrested and condemned, yet entered as publicly as possible. This broke with His earlier habit of avoiding publicity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Remigius (in Aquinas's *Catena Aurea*, a collection of Church Fathers' comments) calls Bethphage a small village of priests on the slope of Olivet, where priests stayed when not serving in the temple. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik, quoting Carson: Jesus rode the colt, an unbroken animal that stayed calm in the excited crowd under the Messiah who controls nature. France suggests the mother came along to reassure the young colt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Ellicott: the order shows Jesus deliberately fulfilling the prophecy. They were to claim the right to use the beasts as for the service of a King, not to hire or ask permission. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/matthew-21.html

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon (via Guzik) is struck that "the Lord" and "has need" appear side by side: Jesus took on a nature full of needs but stayed sovereign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Ellicott lists three possible meanings of "the Lord": God himself, Christ as His disciples called Him, or simply "the Master." He prefers the second. He thinks the owners were probably disciples themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/21.htm
- Spurgeon says the owner was either a secret disciple or held in some awe of Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary-spurgeon
- Chrysostom (in the *Catena*) sees this as no small thing: it showed Jesus could have restrained the Jews but chose not to. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik: Jesus came humbly, on a colt rather than a general's horse, as the Prince of Peace. He adds that "many feel" this day fulfilled Daniel's Seventy Weeks prophecy exactly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Spurgeon: the prophecy shows Zion's King meek even in triumph, riding, not upon a war-horse, but upon a young ass. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary-spurgeon
- In the *Catena*, Pseudo-Chrysostom (a work once credited to Chrysostom) says Christ is "meek" so that He is loved rather than feared for His power. Augustine explains why Matthew's wording of the prophecy differs from John's: the evangelists keep the meaning while varying the words. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html

**vv. 6–7: "Jesus sat on them"** (a real point of debate)
- Most say "them" means the cloaks, not both animals. Ellicott: Jesus rode the colt and the mother walked alongside. https://biblehub.com/matthew/21-7.htm The Geneva Bible notes, the Reformed Bible of 1587, agree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/21-7.htm Constable agrees too. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-7.html
- The Pulpit Commentary rejects Alford's idea that "them" means the animals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/21-7.htm
- Gill leaves it open: one animal, both in turn, or the clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-7.html
- Adam Clarke prefers an ancient manuscript reading, "upon *him*" (the colt). He mentions, without accepting it, an allegory: the tied mother stands for Jews under the Law, the untied colt for Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-7.html
- Jerome thought Jesus could not have ridden both over so short a distance, so he read the scene figuratively. Remigius replies that riding both was possible. Jerome's allegory: the broken-in donkey is the synagogue, the wild colt the Gentiles. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html
- Precept Austin sees Jesus riding an unbroken colt through cheering crowds as evidence of His mastery over creation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary

**v. 8**
- Guzik: spreading cloaks was an act of loyalty, as for Jehu in 2 Kings 9:13. Clarke says branches signalled victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Paul Apple reads the branches as a hope for military victory over Rome, not a gentle symbol of peace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary
- Vincent notes the Greek means "the greater part of the crowd" rather than "a very great crowd." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/21-7.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: "Hosanna" means "save now!" and was addressed to kings. "Son of David" and "He who comes" are titles of the Messiah. Carson notes it later became a shout of praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Jerome explains "Hosanna" as pure Hebrew from Psalm 118:25. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html
- Spurgeon warns that the same crowd soon shouted "Crucify him." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/

**vv. 10–11**
- France (via Guzik): "all Jerusalem" was troubled when the Magi came (2:3), and now the city is stirred again. Trapp observes the crowd didn't know Jesus was born in Bethlehem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Jerome links "the prophet" to the prophet like Moses. Rabanus notes the timing: the Passover lamb was chosen on the tenth day of the month, five days before Passover, the same timing as this entry. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik: this seems to be a different event from John 2. The merchants worked with the priests to overcharge visitors. Jesus drove out buyers as well as sellers. France thinks no lasting reform followed, so the act was an acted parable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Spurgeon (Baptist) says only Christ's hand can truly purify a church, not "Acts of Parliament" or reform societies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Pseudo-Chrysostom: as a good physician, Christ goes first to the source of the city's sickness, the temple and priesthood. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/catena1.ii.xxi.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: the market filled the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Mark's fuller quotation, "for all nations," shows the point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the blind and lame were kept out of the inner courts. After clearing the court, Jesus turned to compassionate healing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik sees hypocrisy: greed in the temple didn't bother the leaders, but praise of Jesus did. Clarke says children often took part in public acclamations of rabbis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Precept Austin: the children crying out praises to God in the temple proved to be wiser than the wise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary

**v. 17**
- Bethany was the home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus, about two miles from Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary

**vv. 18–19**
- On timing, Precept Austin notes that Matthew compresses events. Mark shows the temple cleansing was on Monday and the withering was noticed a day later, which supports reading the tree as a picture of Israel's future. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary
- Spurgeon: fig trees bear fruit before leaves, so a tree in full leaf promised fruit. Like Jerusalem, it was full of religious show but lacked repentance and faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary-spurgeon
- Ellicott says fig trees in Palestine bear two or three crops a year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/matthew-21.html
- Readings of what the tree stands for:
  - Mark Moore: the Jewish leaders. Akin: the fig tree story frames the temple story, showing Jesus cursed the temple and did not just cleanse it. Another comment quoted on the page applies it to unfruitful "Christians" with no real faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary
  - Guzik: Israel's leaders, who talked righteousness but bore no fruit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/

**v. 20**
- Spurgeon: We marvel that they marveled. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary-spurgeon
- Mark shows Peter spoke for the group. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-11-commentary

**v. 21: is the mountain literal or figurative?**
- Guzik: the miracle came from a prayer made in faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-21/
- Barnes: "removing mountains" was a Jewish saying for overcoming difficulties. He also thinks it was literally true for those given the faith of miracles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-21.html
- Matthew Henry: Jewish teachers who could solve great difficulties were praised as "removers of mountains." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-21.html
- Barclay: It is abundantly clear that these promises are not to be taken physically and literally. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-22.html
- Akin (on Precept Austin) calls it hyperbole for what looks impossible. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-21-commentary
- Spurgeon presses believers: if we have never spoken to our mountains, where is our faith? https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64330/

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: there is an unstated condition that the request agrees with God's will. https://biblehub.com/matthew/21-22.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the condition is "stringent." The Greek "the prayer" may point to the Lord's Prayer or early public worship. https://biblehub.com/matthew/21-22.htm
- Constable: God grants requests that agree with His will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-22.html
- A Pulpit homily: the prayer of faith is answered with what God sees best, not always what we name. https://biblehub.com/sermons/matthew/21-22.htm
- Light of Israel commentary takes a stronger faith line: if we believe as if it were done, it is done. But it adds that faith must rest on God's word and will, not our wants. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/21-22.html
- Gotquestions has an article on "have faith and do not doubt," but I only saw the heading, not its argument. https://www.gotquestions.org/have-faith-and-do-not-doubt.html

## What I couldn't find
- **v. 23:** nothing read.
- **Differences between Protestant traditions:** I found no clear disagreement in the pages I read. The main differences are between individual writers: whether Jesus sat on one or both animals (v. 7), and whether the mountain is literal (v. 21). I didn't read any Methodist (Wesley, Seedbed), Lutheran, Pentecostal or Reformed-site pages directly.
- **Modern scholarship:** only one NET Bible note (about Bethphage), quoted on Precept Austin. I didn't read Bible Odyssey.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I only have the Church Fathers in Aquinas's *Catena Aurea*. I didn't read New Advent, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Prosperity / word of faith:** no source found that describes or assesses it on vv. 21–22.
